API: Application Programming Interface: a defined set of requests and responses that lets one piece of software use another.
SDK: Software Development Kit: a bundle of libraries, tools, and docs for building software on a specific platform or service.
SSH: Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for logging into and running commands on a remote machine.
HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request/response protocol web browsers and servers use to exchange data.
DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's directory that translates domain names like example.com into IP addresses.
TCP: Transmission Control Protocol: a network protocol that delivers data reliably and in order between two machines.
REST: Representational State Transfer: a style of web API design built around resources, URLs, and standard HTTP methods.
JSON: JavaScript Object Notation: a lightweight text format for structured data made of objects, arrays, strings, and numbers.
SQL: Structured Query Language: the standard language for querying and modifying relational databases.
CI/CD: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery: automatically building, testing, and shipping code whenever changes are pushed.
CPU: Central Processing Unit: the general-purpose processor that executes a computer's instructions.
GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: a processor with thousands of parallel cores, widely used to train and run neural networks.
TPU: Tensor Processing Unit: Google's custom chip designed specifically to accelerate machine learning workloads.
CUDA: NVIDIA's platform and API for running general-purpose computations on its GPUs.
container: A lightweight, isolated package of an application and its dependencies that runs consistently across environments.
Kubernetes: An open-source system for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications across clusters of machines.
latency: The delay between a request being made and its response arriving, usually measured in milliseconds.
cache: A fast storage layer that keeps copies of frequently used data so future requests are served quicker.
hashing: Mapping data of any size to a fixed-size value, used for lookups, integrity checks, and password storage.
encryption: Encoding data so that only parties holding the right key can read it.
compiler: A program that translates source code into machine code or another lower-level form before it runs.
recursion: A technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances of the same problem.
AI: Artificial Intelligence: the field of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence.
ML: Machine Learning: building systems that learn patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
machine learning: Building systems that learn patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
deep learning: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers to learn increasingly abstract features from data.
neural network: A model made of layers of interconnected nodes whose weighted connections are tuned from data.
LLM: Large Language Model: a neural network trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate language.
NLP: Natural Language Processing: the field of getting computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
transformer: A neural network architecture built on attention, the basis of most modern language models.
attention: A mechanism that lets a model weigh how relevant each part of the input is when processing another part.
embedding: A list of numbers (a vector) representing an item such as a word or document so that similar items sit close together.
vector database: A database optimized for storing embeddings and quickly finding the vectors most similar to a query.
token: A chunk of text, often a word or word piece, that a language model reads and generates one at a time.
tokenizer: The component that splits raw text into tokens and maps them to numeric IDs for a model.
context window: The maximum number of tokens a language model can take into account at once.
prompt: The input text or instructions given to a generative AI model to steer its output.
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetching relevant documents at query time and giving them to an LLM so its answer is grounded in them.
inference: Running a trained model on new inputs to produce predictions or outputs, as opposed to training it.
training: The process of adjusting a model's parameters on data so its predictions improve.
fine-tuning: Further training a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialize it.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation: a fine-tuning method that trains small add-on matrices instead of all of a model's weights.
quantization: Storing a model's weights with fewer bits (e.g. 8 or 4 instead of 16) to shrink it and speed up inference.
distillation: Training a smaller "student" model to imitate a larger "teacher" model's outputs.
hallucination: When a generative model produces confident-sounding output that is false or not supported by its input.
overfitting: When a model memorizes its training data so closely that it performs poorly on new, unseen data.
gradient descent: An optimization method that repeatedly nudges parameters in the direction that most reduces the error.
backpropagation: The algorithm that computes how much each weight in a neural network contributed to the error, so it can be updated.
loss function: A formula that scores how wrong a model's predictions are; training tries to minimize it.
epoch: One complete pass through the entire training dataset.
hyperparameter: A setting chosen before training, like learning rate or batch size, rather than learned from data.
benchmark: A standardized test or dataset used to measure and compare the performance of systems or models.
CNN: Convolutional Neural Network: a network that uses sliding filters to detect patterns, commonly used for images.
RNN: Recurrent Neural Network: a network that processes sequences step by step while carrying a hidden state forward.
GAN: Generative Adversarial Network: two networks, a generator and a discriminator, trained against each other to produce realistic data.
diffusion model: A generative model that creates data, such as images, by learning to gradually remove noise from random input.
reinforcement learning: Training an agent by rewarding or penalizing its actions as it interacts with an environment.
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: tuning a model using human preference ratings as the reward signal.
agent: An AI system that plans and takes actions, such as calling tools or APIs, to accomplish a goal.
